Ishmael murders Gedaliah (verses 1–10)

People who hate God's worshipers sometimes pretend to be godly in order to harm them more easily.

Death often arrives where it is least expected.

We should therefore continually examine whether our hearts and lives are in the condition we would wish to be found in when summoned before our Judge.

Sometimes a person's riches can obtain a temporary escape from deadly danger.

Yet those who imagine they can bribe death itself, saying, “Do not kill us; we have treasure hidden in the fields,” are terribly mistaken.

This sorrowful history warns us never to suppose that we are completely safe in this world.

We cannot be certain of uninterrupted peace until we reach heaven.

Johanan rescues the captives but plans to flee (verses 11–18)

The success of wickedness is short-lived.

No one can truly prosper by hardening the heart against God.

Those who make excuses for sinful choices by pretending to fear a danger may then justly lose comfort because of real dangers.

A wise and peaceful ruler may be removed, only for a rash and ambitious person to rise in that ruler's place.

Such changes deeply affect the welfare of many people.

Only those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways can enjoy lasting steadiness and true happiness.

Verses 1-10 Those who hate the worshippers of God, often put on the appearance of piety, that they may the easier hurt them. As death often meets men where they least expect it, we should continually search whether we are in such a state and frame of mind, as we would wish to be found in when called to appear before our Judge. Sometimes the ransom of a man's life is his riches. But those who think to bribe death, saying, Slay us not, for we have treasures in the field, will find themselves wretchedly deceived. This melancholy history warns us, never to be secure in this world. We never can be sure of peace on this side heaven.
[Jer.41.11-Jer.41.18]
Verses 11-18 The success of villany must be short, and none can prosper who harden their hearts against God. And those justly lose comfort in real fears, who excuse themselves in sin by pretended fears. The removal of a prudent and peaceable ruler, and the succession of another who is rash and ambitious, affects the welfare of many. Only those are happy and steady who fear the Lord and walk in his ways.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJohanan desires Jeremiah to ask counsel of God.1–6They are assured of safety in Judea, but of destruction in Egypt.7–22
Johanan asks Jeremiah to seek God's counsel (verses 1–6)

The commanders sought Jeremiah's help when it suited their purposes.

Whenever we face difficult or uncertain choices, we should look to God for direction.

We may pray in faith for the Spirit's wisdom within our hearts and guidance through God's Providence.

But we do not genuinely desire to know God's will unless we have already resolved to obey what he reveals.

Many promise to do whatever the Lord commands while inwardly hoping that his answer will flatter their pride and leave their favorite sins untouched.

Something will eventually expose the true condition of their hearts.

God's answer commands them to remain in Judah (verses 7–22)

If we wish to know God's will in doubtful circumstances, we must wait as well as pray.

He is ready to show mercy again to those he has corrected.

He rejects no one who trusts his promises.

His word gives enough encouragement to calm even the unreasonable fears that keep his people from their duties.

Whatever loss or hardship obedience may appear to bring, God's promises provide for it.

He will protect and deliver those who trust and serve him.

It is folly to leave the place where our duty lies merely because we meet trouble there, especially when doing so means abandoning the land God had set apart.

The very dangers we hope to avoid through sin are often brought upon us by the sin itself.

This applies to ordinary life as well.

Someone may hope to escape human suffering by moving elsewhere. Yet the troubles common to humanity will follow wherever that person goes.

Those who make solemn promises to God while deliberately hiding their intentions deserve serious rebuke.

Their conduct reveals more than their words.

We do not always know what is truly good for us.

What we most eagerly desire and cling to may prove harmful—or even fatal.
classic_reading:
[Jer.42.1-Jer.42.6]
Chapter 42
Johanan desires Jeremiah to ask counsel of God. ( [Jer.42.1-Jer.42.6] Jr 42:1-6) They are assured of safety in Judea, but of destruction in Egypt. ( [Jer.42.7-Jer.42.22] Jr 42:7-22)
Verses 1-6 To serve a turn, Jeremiah is sought out, and the captains ask for his assistance. In every difficult, doubtful case, we must look to God for direction; and we may still, in faith, pray to be guided by a spirit of wisdom in our hearts, and the leadings of Providence. We do not truly desire to know the mind of God, if we do not fully resolve to comply with it when we know it. Many promise to do what the Lord requires, while they hope to have their pride flattered, and their favourite lusts spared. Yet something betrays the state of their hearts.
[Jer.42.7-Jer.42.22]
Verses 7-22 If we would know the mind of the Lord in doubtful cases, we must wait as well as pray. God is ever ready to return in mercy to those he has afflicted; and he never rejects any who rely on his promises. He has declared enough to silence even the causeless fears of his people, which discourge them in the way of duty. Whatever loss or suffering we may fear from obedience, is provided against in God's word; and he will protect and deliver all who trust in him and serve him. It is folly to quit our place, especially to quit a holy land, because we meet with trouble in it. And the evils we think to escape by sin, we certainly bring upon ourselves. We may apply this to the common troubles of life; and those who think to avoid them by changing their place, will find that the grievances common to men will meet them wherever they go. Sinners who dissemble with God in solemn professions especially should be rebuked with sharpness; for their actions speak more plainly than words. We know not what is good for ourselves; and what we are most fond of, and have our hearts most set upon, often proves hurtful, and sometimes fatal.

The leaders take the people into Egypt (verses 1–7)

Pride produces conflict, both with God and with other people.

The leaders preferred their own wisdom to God's revealed will.

People often deny that Scripture is God's word because they have already decided not to submit to its commands.

When someone is determined to continue in sin, that person may even assign evil motives to the best actions.

These Jews abandoned their own land and took themselves outside the protection God had promised there.

How foolish people can be: in attempting to improve their circumstances through disobedience, they bring disaster upon themselves.

Jeremiah foretells Egypt's conquest (verses 8–13)

God can find his people wherever they are.

The Spirit of prophecy was not confined to Israel's territory.

Jeremiah announced that Nebuchadnezzar would conquer Egypt and take many Egyptians captive.

God sometimes uses one wicked person or nation to judge another.

He will also punish those who mislead people professing to belong to him or tempt them to rebel against his commands.

The leaders carry the people to Egypt. ( [Jer.43.1-Jer.43.7] Jr 43:1-7) Jeremiah foretells the conquest of Egypt. ( [Jer.43.8-Jer.43.13] Jr 43:8-13)
Verses 1-7 Only by pride comes contention, both with God and man. They preferred their own wisdom to the revealed will of God. Men deny the Scriptures to be the word of God, because they are resolved not to conform themselves to Scripture rules. When men will persist in sin, they charge the best actions to bad motives. These Jews deserted their own land, and threw themselves out of God's protection. It is the folly of men, that they often ruin themselves by wrong endeavours to mend their situation.
[Jer.43.8-Jer.43.13]
Verses 8-13 God can find his people wherever they are. The Spirit of prophecy was not confined to the land of Israel. It is foretold that Nebuchadnezzar should destroy and carry into captivity many of the Egyptians. Thus God makes one wicked man, or wicked nation, a scourge and plague to another. He will punish those who deceive his professing people, or tempt them to rebellion.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Jews in Egypt persist in idolatry.1–14They refuse to reform.15–19Jeremiah then denounces destruction upon them.20–30
The Jews in Egypt persist in idolatry (verses 1–14)

God reminded the Jews that Judah's earlier sins had brought about the country's destruction.

We ought to warn others earnestly about the danger of sin:

Do not do it!

If you love God, do not sin, because it provokes him.

If you love your own soul, do not sin, because it destroys you.

Let conscience speak to us in this way whenever we are tempted.

The Jews whom God had sent into the land of the Chaldeans were, through his grace, being drawn away from idolatry.

But those who had deliberately gone into Egypt against his command became even more attached to idols.

When we enter situations of temptation without reason or divine calling, it is just for God to leave us to the consequences of our own choices.

If we walk against him, he will walk against us.

The greatest and most dreadful misery people experience arises from neglecting the salvation offered to them.

The people refuse to reform (verses 15–19)

These bold sinners did not even attempt to excuse themselves.

They openly declared that they intended to continue doing what God forbade.

People who knowingly disobey God often become steadily worse; sin deceives and hardens their hearts.

Their words reveal the true attitude of a rebellious heart.

Even afflictions that ought to have separated them from idolatry were interpreted by them as reasons to keep practicing it.

It is terrible when people who ought to encourage one another toward God and heaven instead encourage one another in sin and thereby prepare one another for judgment.

Combining idolatry with the worship of God and rejecting the mediation of Christ provoke God and bring ruin upon people.

Henry extends this warning against idolatry to the worship of images and what he regards as religious honors wrongly paid to saints, angels and the queen of heaven. This is his own theological application of the passage, preserved as such rather than presented as a new statement of the biblical narrative.

He urges readers to remember what happened because of the Jews' idolatrous practices.

Jeremiah announces judgment (verses 20–30)

When evil comes upon us, we should consider how we have sinned against the Lord.

We should stand in awe of him and turn from sin.

Since these people were determined to remain in idolatry, God would continue judging them.

Even the little true religion still present among them would disappear.

The earthly comforts and sources of security in which we place our greatest confidence may fail just as quickly as those in which we place little trust.

They are what God makes them, not what we imagine them to be.

A well-founded hope of sharing God's mercy is always joined with repentance and obedience.
classic_reading:
[Jer.44.1-Jer.44.14]
Chapter 44
The Jews in Egypt persist in idolatry. ( [Jer.44.1-Jer.44.14] Jr 44:1-14) They refuse to reform. ( [Jer.44.15-Jer.44.19] Jr 44:15-19) Jeremiah then denounces destruction upon them. ( [Jer.44.20-Jer.44.30] Jr 44:20-30)
Verses 1-14 God reminds the Jews of the sins that brought desolations upon Judah. It becomes us to warn men of the danger of sin with all seriousness: Oh, do not do it! If you love God, do not, for it is provoking to him; if you love your own souls, do not, for it is destructive to them. Let conscience do this for us in the hour of temptation. The Jews whom God sent into the land of the Chaldeans, were there, by the power of God's grace, weaned from idolatry; but those who went by their own perverse will into the land of the Egyptians, were there more attached than ever to their idolatries. When we thrust ourselves without cause or call into places of temptation, it is just with God to leave us to ourselves. If we walk contrary to God, he will walk contrary to us. The most awful miseries to which men are exposed, are occasioned by the neglect of offered salvation.
[Jer.44.15-Jer.44.19]
Verses 15-19 These daring sinners do not attempt excuses, but declare they will do that which is forbidden. Those who disobey God, commonly grow worse and worse, and the heart is more hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Here is the real language of the rebellious heart. Even the afflictions which should have parted them from their sins, were taken so as to confirm them in their sins. It is sad when those who should quicken each other to what is good, and so help one another to heaven, harden each other in sin, and so ripen one another for hell. To mingle idolatry with Divine worship, and to reject the mediation of Christ, are provoking to God, and ruinous to men. All who worship images, or honour saints, and angels, and the queen of heaven, should recollect what came from the idolatrous practices of the Jews.
[Jer.44.20-Jer.44.30]
Verses 20-30 Whatever evil comes upon us, it is because we have sinned against the Lord; we should therefore stand in awe, and sin not. Since they were determined to persist in their idolatry, God would go on to punish them. What little remains of religion were among them, would be lost. The creature-comforts and confidences from which we promise ourselves most, may fail as soon as those from which we promise ourselves least; and all are what God makes them, not what we fancy them to be. Well-grounded hopes of our having a part in the Divine mercy, are always united with repentance and obedience.

modern_osis:
Original heading

An encouragement sent to Baruch.

God's correction and encouragement for Baruch

Baruch had written Jeremiah's prophecies and read them aloud, as described in Jeremiah 36.

The king threatened him because of that service.

People who are just beginning to serve the Lord are often discouraged by difficulties that are small compared with what may come later.

These complaints and fears arise from the corruption remaining in their hearts.

Baruch had expected too much from earthly life, making the suffering he faced far harder to endure.

The world's hostility would not trouble us so much if we had not foolishly hoped for its approval and eagerly sought its favor.

How foolish to seek great things for ourselves here, where everything is small and nothing is secure!

The Lord understands the real reasons for our anxiety and discouragement better than we understand them ourselves.

Let us ask him to examine our hearts and restrain every disordered desire within them.
classic_reading:
[Jer.45.1]
Chapter 45
An encouragement sent to Baruch.
Baruch was employed in writing Jeremiah's prophecies, and reading them, see Jr 36, and was threatened for it by the king. Young beginners in religion are apt to be discouraged with little difficulties, which they commonly meet with at first in the service of God. These complaints and fears came from his corruptions. Baruch had raised his expectations too high in this world, and that made the distress and trouble he was in harder to be borne. The frowns of the world would not disquiet us, if we did not foolishly flatter ourselves with the hopes of its smiles, and court and covet them. What a folly is it then to seek great things for ourselves here, where every thing is little, and nothing certain! The Lord knows the real cause of our fretfulness and despondency better than we do, and we should beg of him to examine our hearts, and to repress every wrong desire in us.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe defeat of the Egyptians.1–12Their overthrow after the siege of Tyre.13–26A promise of comfort to the Jews.27, 28
The Egyptians are defeated (verses 1–12)

The whole word of God speaks against those who refuse to obey the gospel of Christ.

But it speaks for everyone who turns to him, including those from the nations outside Israel.

The prophecy begins with Egypt.

Let the Egyptians strengthen themselves with every skill, ally and resource they possess: their efforts will be useless.

The wounds God inflicts upon his enemies cannot be healed by ordinary medicines.

In this ever-changing world, strength and prosperity soon pass from one person or nation to another.

Egypt is judged, while Israel receives comfort (verses 13–28)

Those who seized what belonged to other people would now find their own land invaded.

Egypt resembled a beautiful heifer not accustomed to bearing the yoke of subjection.

But destruction would come from the north: the Chaldeans were coming.

At the same time, God announced comfort and peace to the Israel of God.

Those promises encouraged his people while judgments were falling upon surrounding nations.

He would remain with them and correct them in measure.

He would not subject them to everlasting destruction away from his presence.

Verses 1-12 The whole word of God is against those who obey not the gospel of Christ; but it is for those, even of the Gentiles, who turn to Him. The prophecy begins with Egypt. Let them strengthen themselves with all the art and interest they have, yet it shall be all in vain. The wounds God inflicts on his enemies, cannot be healed by medicines. Power and prosperity soon pass from one to another in this changing world.

He will be with them, and only correct them in measure; and will not punish them with everlasting destruction from his presence.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The calamities of the Philistines.

The Philistines face judgment

The Philistines had long been enemies of Israel.

The Chaldean army would now sweep over their territory like a great flood.

When God determines to bring a people down, no one can prevent it.

When he intends to destroy the wicked, he can remove every source of assistance they rely upon.

The devastation caused by war is so dreadful that peace should be highly valued.

Yet we must submit to the Lord's appointments, because he orders everything with perfect wisdom and justice.
classic_reading:
[Jer.47.1]
Chapter 47
The calamities of the Philistines.
The Philistines had always been enemies to Israel; but the Chaldean army shall overflow their land like a deluge. Those whom God will spoil, must be spoiled. For when the Lord intends to destroy the wicked, he will cut off every helper. So deplorable are the desolations of war, that the blessings of peace are most desirable. But we must submit to His appointments who ordains all in perfect wisdom and justice.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesProphecies against Moab for pride and security.1–13For carnal confidence and contempt of God.14–47
Moab's proud security ends in ruin (verses 1–13)

The Chaldeans would destroy Moab.

We should be thankful that our calling is to seek the salvation of people's lives and souls, not to shed their blood.

But that privilege makes us all the more accountable if we perform such a good work deceitfully or carelessly.

Moab's cities would become ruins, and its countryside would be laid waste.

There would be great sorrow and confusion.

Even if sinners could be given wings, they still could not fly beyond the reach of God's righteous judgment.

Many people persist in wrongdoing without repenting, yet continue to enjoy outward prosperity for a long time.

The Moabites had remained corrupt and unchanged, secure and devoted to bodily pleasure.

They had not experienced disruptions to their prosperity, and therefore their hearts and lives remained unchanged (Psalm 55:19).

Moab is warned, yet restoration is promised (verses 14–47)

The prophecy continues describing Moab's destruction.

These warnings were intended to awaken national repentance and reform that might prevent the disaster, or at least personal repentance and reform to prepare individuals for it.

As we read this long list of threats and the terrifying figures used to express them, it is more profitable to reflect on the power of God's anger and the justice of his judgments than to become preoccupied with explaining every image.

The destruction, however, would not be permanent.

The chapter ends by promising that Moab's captivity would be reversed in the latter days.

God would not contend even with the Moabites forever.

Henry reports that Jewish interpreters connected this promise with the days of the Messiah.

In that larger application, people from the nations who are held in bondage to sin and Satan are brought back by divine grace and become truly free.
classic_reading:
[Jer.48.1-Jer.48.13]
Chapter 48
Prophecies against Moab for pride and security. ( [Jer.48.1-Jer.48.13] Jr 48:1-13) For carnal confidence and contempt of God. ( [Jer.48.14-Jer.48.47] Jr 48:14-47)
Verses 1-13 . The Chaldeans are to destroy the Moabites. We should be thankful that we are required to seek the salvation of men's lives, and the salvation of their souls, not to shed their blood; but we shall be the more without excuse if we do this pleasant work deceitfully. The cities shall be laid in ruins, and the country shall be wasted. There will be great sorrow. There will be great hurry. If any could give wings to sinners, still they could not fly out of the reach of Divine indignation. There are many who persist in unrepented iniquity, yet long enjoy outward prosperity. They had been long corrupt and unreformed, secure and sensual in prosperity. They have no changes of their peace and prosperity, therefore their hearts and lives are unchanged, Ps. 55:19.
[Jer.48.14-Jer.48.47]
Verses 14-47 . The destruction of Moab is further prophesied, to awaken them by national repentance and reformation to prevent the trouble, or by a personal repentance and reformation to prepare for it. In reading this long roll of threatenings, and mediating on the terror, it will be of more use to us to keep in view the power of God's anger and the terror of his judgments, and to have our hearts possessed with a holy awe of God and of his wrath, than to search into all the figures and expressions here used. Yet it is not perpetual destruction. The chapter ends with a promise of their return out of captivity in the latter days. Even with Moabites God will not contend for ever, nor be always wroth. The Jews refer it to the days of the Messiah; then the captives of the Gentiles, under the yoke of sin and Satan, shall be brought back by Divine grace, which shall make them free indeed.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesProphecies relative to the Ammonites.1–6The Edomites.7–22The Syrians.23–27The Kedarenes.28–33The Elamites.34–39
The Ammonites face judgment (verses 1–6)

Among human beings, power often wins against what is right.

But the Almighty governs even powerful people and judges fairly.

Like the Ammonites, those who suppose everything they can seize must rightfully belong to them will discover their error.

The Lord calls people to account for every dishonest act, especially offenses committed against those who have no resources or defenders.

Judgment comes upon Edom (verses 7–22)

The Edomites were longstanding enemies of God's Israel.

Their day of judgment had now drawn near.

The warning concerned them, but it was also given for the sake of God's people, whose suffering the Edomites had made worse.

Divine judgment moves from nation to nation.

The earth is full of upheaval, and no one can escape the agents God appoints to execute his just purposes.

Even amid human violence, we should recognize the Lord's righteousness.

Syria and Damascus are humbled (verses 23–27)

How easily God can take away the courage of nations celebrated for their bravery!

Damascus became weak.

It had been a joyful city with many of the pleasures people desire.

But those who place their happiness in earthly and bodily enjoyment deceive themselves.

Kedar is scattered (verses 28–33)

Nebuchadnezzar would devastate the people of Kedar, who lived in the deserts of Arabia.

A ruler who had captured many strong cities would not spare those who lived in tents.

He acted to satisfy his own greed and ambition.

Yet God directed the events to correct an ungrateful people and warn a careless world that danger can arrive when it feels most secure.

The inhabitants would flee far away, withdrawing into the depths of the desert and becoming scattered.

But privacy and obscurity do not always bring safety.

Elam is judged, but not abandoned forever (verses 34–39)

Henry identifies the Elamites with the Persians; that is his historical identification in this commentary.

They had acted against God's Israel and would be called to account.

Evil pursues those who practice sin.

God would show them that he reigns.

Nevertheless, Elam's destruction would not last forever.

Henry understands the promise of restoration as finding its full realization in the days of the Messiah.

When believers read God's warnings against the enemies of his church, they can take courage that the result of the spiritual conflict is not uncertain.

The One who is for us is greater than all who oppose us.

He will subdue the enemies of our souls.

[Jer.49.7-Jer.49.22]
Verses 7-22 The Edomites were old enemies to the Israel of God. But their day is now at hand; it is foretold, not only to warn them, but for the sake of the Israel of God, whose afflictions were aggravated by them. Thus Divine judgments go round from nation to nation; the earth is full of commotion, and nothing can escape the ministers of Divine vengeance. The righteousness of God is to be observed amidst the violence of men.

Verses 23-27 How easily God can dispirit those nations that have been most celebrated for valour! Damascus waxes feeble. It was a city of joy, having all the delights of the sons of men. But those deceive themselves who place their happiness in carnal joys.

Verses 28-33 Nebuchadnezzar would make desolation among the people of Kedar, who dwelt in the deserts of Arabia. He will do this to gratify his own covetousness and ambition; but God orders it for correcting an unthankful people, and for warning a careless world to expect trouble when they seem most safe. Verses 34-39 The Elamites were the Persians; they acted against God's Israel, and must be reckoned with. Evil pursues sinners. God will make them know that he reigns. In reading the Divine assurance of the destruction of all the enemies of the church, the believer sees that the issue of the holy war is not doubtful. It is blessed to recollect, that He who is for us, is more than all against us. And he will subdue the enemies of our souls.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe ruin of Babylon.1–3, 8–16, 21–32, 35–46The redemption of God's people.4–7, 17–20, 33–34
Babylon's downfall and God's people's return (verses 1–7)

The Babylonian king had treated Jeremiah with kindness.

Yet the prophet was still obliged to announce the destruction of that king's empire.

When those friendly toward us are enemies of God, we must not proclaim a false peace to them.

Babylon's destruction is described as thorough and final.

But within these warnings comes comfort for the Jews.

They would return first to their God, and then to their country.

The promise of their conversion and reform prepares the way for the other blessings promised to them.

Their tears would no longer be merely the grief of worldly losses, as when they went into captivity, but godly sorrow over sin.

They would seek the Lord as their God and abandon idols.

Then they would think of returning to their homeland.

This illustrates the return of lost souls to God.

Genuine converts sincerely desire to reach the right end and continually take care to remain on the right path.

The condition of the people before their restoration was truly sorrowful.

Even when professing Christians commit sins, those sins never justify others' pleasure in persecuting or destroying them.

Verified editorial cross-reference: Jer.50.1-Jer.50.3; Jer.50.8-Jer.50.16; Jer.50.21-Jer.50.32; Jer.50.35-Jer.50.46.Verified editorial cross-reference: Jer.50.4-Jer.50.7; Jer.50.17-Jer.50.20; Jer.50.33; Jer.50.34.
Babylon is devastated and Israel regathered (verses 8–20)

Babylon's devastation is described through many images.

The Lord's anger against sin is its underlying cause.

The nation would be laid waste because it had rebelled against God.

Sin makes people targets for the arrows of divine judgment.

The mercy promised to the Israel of God would not merely come after Babylon's destruction: its deliverance would arise through that destruction.

The scattered sheep would be gathered from the wilderness and returned to good pasture.

Everyone who returns to God and to duty discovers true satisfaction of soul.

Deliverance from suffering becomes real comfort when it comes as a fruit of forgiven sin.

God's forces bring Babylon low (verses 21–32)

Forces would be gathered and given the power to destroy Babylon.

By carrying out the task God appointed, they would bring to pass what he had announced.

Pride causes God to oppose a person and quickly brings ruin nearer.

Babylon's own arrogance would be its downfall.

She had proudly opposed the Holy One of Israel.

Who can preserve in power those whom God has determined to bring down?

The weak have a mighty Redeemer (verses 33–46)

Israel could take comfort in knowing that although God's people were weak, their Redeemer was strong.

This applies to believers who struggle under the power of sin and corruption and feel the weight of their weakness and many shortcomings.

Their Redeemer is able to guard what they entrust to him.

Sin will not have dominion over them.

He will give them the rest that remains for God's people.

Babylon's wrongdoing and punishment are also described.

Her central sins included idolatry and persecution.

The Lord does not save his people so they can remain in their sins, and he will certainly not approve the wickedness of their declared enemies.

Judgment for Babylon's sins would leave the country desolate.

When we read about prosperous Babylon's destruction and afflicted Israel's rescue, we learn to choose suffering with God's people rather than brief enjoyment of the pleasures of sin.
classic_reading:
[Jer.50.1-Jer.50.7]
Chapter 50
The ruin of Babylon. ( [Jer.50.1-Jer.3.8] Jr 50:1-3,8-16,21-32,35-46;) The redemption of God's people. ( [Jer.50.4-Jer.7.17] Jr 50:4-7,17-20,33,34)
Verses 1-7 The king of Babylon was kind to Jeremiah, yet the prophet must foretell the ruin of that kingdom. If our friends are God's enemies, we dare not speak peace to them. The destruction of Babylon is spoken of as done thoroughly. Here is a word for the comfort of the Jews. They shall return to their God first, then to their own land; the promise of their conversion and reformation makes way for the other promises. Their tears flow not from the sorrow of the world, as when they went into captivity, but from godly sorrow. They shall seek after the Lord as their God, and have no more to do with idols. They shall think of returning to their own country. This represents the return of poor souls to God. In true converts there are sincere desires to attain the end, and constant cares to keep in the way. Their present case is lamented as very sad. The sins of professing Christians never will excuse those who rejoice in destroying them.
[Jer.50.8-Jer.50.20]
Verses 8-20 The desolation that shall be brought upon Babylon is set forth in a variety of expressions. The cause of this destruction is the wrath of the Lord. Babylon shall be wholly desolated; for she hath sinned against the Lord. Sin makes men a mark for the arrows of God's judgments. The mercy promised to the Israel of God, shall not only accompany, but arise from the destruction of Babylon. These sheep shall be gathered from the deserts, and put again into good pasture. All who return to God and their duty, shall find satisfaction of soul in so doing. Deliverances out of trouble are comforts indeed, when fruits of the forgiveness of sin.
[Jer.50.21-Jer.50.32]
Verses 21-32 The forces are mustered and empowered to destroy Babylon. Let them do what God demands, and they shall bring to pass what he threatens. The pride of men's hearts sets God against them, and ripens them apace for ruin. Babylon's pride must be her ruin; she has been proud against the Holy One of Israel; who can keep those up whom God will throw down?
[Jer.50.33-Jer.50.46]
Verses 33-46 It is Israel's comfort in distress, that, though they are weak, their Redeemer is strong. This may be applied to believers, who complain of the dominion of sin and corruption, and of their own weakness and manifold infirmities. Their Redeemer is able to keep what they commit to him; and sin shall not have dominion over them. He will give them that rest which remains for the people of God. Also here is Babylon's sin, and their punishment. The sins are, idolatry and persecution. He that will not save his people in their sins, never will countenance the wickedness of his open enemies. The judgments of God for these sins will lay them waste. In the judgments denounced against prosperous Babylon, and the mercies promised to afflicted Israel, we learn to choose to suffer affliction with the people of God, rather than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.
